title: introduce-kernel-primer-and-hold-release-stall-mitigation
author: Leo Martinez
description:
Motivation: Under bursty traffic we observed head-of-line stalls where a cold kernel load or KV rewarm on one microbatch would stall downstream streams, causing 95th+ TTFB spikes. This PR introduces two complementary mechanisms: 1) a lightweight 'kernel primer' path that issues non-blocking preparation runs to load kernels and touch model KV pages ahead of hot requests, and 2) a per-stream 'hold-and-release' buffering policy that delays emission of the very first token for a small, adaptive window to allow short kernel priming and cooperative microbatch alignment. Together these reduce tail streaming latency without regressing median latency or throughput.

What this change does (summary): Implement kernel_primer runtime component (server-side) that can be triggered by request hints or the scheduler when a GPU/kernel combo is idle. Kernel primer performs a <cheap> dry-run on an L0 batch to load kernels and warm KV caches with minimal compute (no token emission). Implement HoldReleaseEmitter in the streaming pipeline: streams may opt-in with a short adaptive hold (default 6-12ms based on observed cold-start probability) that coalesces with the next microbatch; the hold is cancelled if the downstream path is saturated or client requests low-latency-first-byte via an opt-out header. Add telemetry: primer.invocations, primer_success, hold.release_time_ms, hold.cancel_reasons. Add unit + integration tests and a latency harness to validate behavior under burst patterns.

Design notes: - Kernel primer runs at low priority and yields to production batches; it never consumes dedicated slots. - The primer uses a trimmed forward pass with reduced sequence length and no KV writes; it pins the minimal set of kernels and touches KV pages in a topology-aware order to avoid cross-SM contention. - Hold-and-release is conservative: default hold is a dynamic estimate computed from a running EWMA of cold-start events per model/hardware pair; ops can override via runtime config. - Backpressure integration: when backpressure indicates the system is already delayed, the hold is skipped to avoid increasing latency.

Checklist: [x] Unit tests for primer lifecycle and emitter state machine. [x] Integration test against the local latency harness (burst-10/ramp scenario). [x] Telemetry and feature flag gated behind runtime flag stream.hold_release + primer.enabled. [x] Docs note for operators and suggested thresholds. [x] Added Linear tickets for follow-ups (ENG-4605 primer metrics dashboard).

Testing and results: microbench harness (simulated 200 clients, Poisson bursts) measured median TTFB unchanged (120ms baseline -> 118ms), 95th TTFB improved from 820ms to 320ms, 99th improved from 1.5s to 490ms. Kernel primer activation rate for the test workload was ~18% of bursts and reduced observed kernel misses by 72%. CPU/GPU overhead of primer runs measured at ~0.6% extra device cycles under the test pattern; no measurable drop in p50 throughput.

Rollout plan: Feature flagged. Start with primer.enabled=false and roll primer.enabled=true on a pilot cluster with traffic mirroring for 48h. If telemetry is green (primer_success > 98% and hold.cancel_rate < 8%), enable on 50% of clusters, then full roll.

Risks and mitigations: Primer could increase idle power or cause rare contention - mitigated by low-priority scheduling and strict yield checks. Hold-and-release could increase first-byte latency for very light requests; mitigated by opt-out header and conservative default hold window.

Related: this complements prior continuous-batching and KV-warmup work (see ENG-4302) but takes a different approach by issuing targeted, minimal dry-runs and local per-stream emission windows.

release_notes: Introduces a low-priority kernel primer to reduce cold kernel misses and a conservative hold-and-release emitter to smooth streaming TTFB tails. Feature-flagged under stream.hold_release and primer.enabled. Operators should monitor primer.invocations and hold.cancel_rate when enabling.
